newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU finance ministers reassured by France on EMU.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers reassured by France on EMU.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, meeting after a turbulent fortnight that has thrown the future of the EU's single currency into doubt, on Sunday dismissed any talk of delaying the project.

The ministers, emerging from a dinner at which they discussed new euro coins, also said the new French government had shown a clear commitment to economic and monetary union (EMU) and the targets set to reach it.
But questions remained over France's stance on the EU's stability pact, which was to be discussed at the ministers' regular monthly session on Monday.
Echoing comments earlier in Germany from Chancellor Helmut Kohl, ministers and other EU officials said putting back the start of EMU was not on the cards.

"The clear underlying message tonight was that EMU was on target," Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said at the end of a dinner with his EU counterparts. "The momentum towards a single currency was being maintained."
The dinner and Monday's meeting have been overshadowed by turmoil in the 15-nation bloc's plans for EMU.

Uncertainty over the new French government and Germany's difficulties in getting its finances in order have left financial and political analysts predicting that EMU will either be delayed from its January 1, 1999 start or will begin with a weaker currency in a broad range of countries.
But the ministers emerged from the meeting saying all was well.
"We confirmed the commitment of each country to respect the treaty," Italian Finance Minster Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said, referring to the Maastricht Treaty setting out the rules for monetary union.
The ministers also said new French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn had reiterated the Socialist government's support for the single currency.

"It's quite clear that the French government is in favour of the EMU process and respecting the treaty of Maastricht. And that's important," Dutch Finance Minster Gerrit Zalm, whose country is EU president, said.
"I don't see why anyone would doubt it," Strauss-Kahn said when asked about the comments.
Ministers also played down the chances of a fight over the so-called stability pact, due to be be ratified formally at a summit in Amsterdam next week, despite French concerns.
The pact, agreed in principle at a summit in Dublin in December, is designed to keep countries from running high deficits once the single currency is introduced.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said during his election campaign he did not feel bound by the pact.
Ministers said the pact had not been discussed over dinner and would be addressed on Monday.

But Luxembourg Finance and Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who had earlier said the pact needed to be made to suit all countries, said he believed it could be ratified at the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
Sunday's talks were the first between German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his counterparts since Bonn floated the idea of revaluing gold reserves to shore up Germany's flagging finances.
It was a move that raised questions about Germany's ability to meet the strict tests of EMU without resorting to creative accounting, something Bonn had sharply criticised others for attempting.
A compromise has been reached between Waigel and the Bundesbank, which vehemently opposed the plan, but Germany's difficulty in meeting EMU criteria has been given a clear public viewing.
Waigel said nothing about the issue to reporters.
